interactive.title: Direct proportion
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on a ratio table, a column for each pair of amounts with the same step written above and below, on two scales locked together for a transformer's primary and secondary voltage, and on rows of blocks, a fixed charge in a light tint and each hour, day or length of cable in solid ink, some screens showing an idea and the rest asking you to try it.
interactive.ignores: The voltages, charges, rates and weights (a 10 : 1 transformer from 0 to 400 V, a £40 call-out with £30 an hour, three firms' prices, a 3 kg cable drum, a van hire) are example values, chosen to show the method. It treats the transformer as ideal: a real one's secondary sits a little lower under load, and a real one is used only up to its rated voltage.

explain.text:
Two amounts are in direct proportion when they grow by the same ×, not by the same amount: if the first is doubled, the other is doubled too.[^1] Multiplying one by any number multiplies the other by the same number, and 0 of one goes with 0 of the other. A transformer's voltages work this way. Its turns ratio is the same as its voltage ratio,[^2] so on a 10 : 1 transformer the secondary voltage stays a tenth of the primary. 100 V in gives 10 V out, 200 V gives 20 V, and 230 V gives 230 ÷ 10 = 23 V. On a ratio table the same × takes one column to the next on both rows, and a rise of 100 V on the primary is a rise of only 10 V on the secondary.

Not every amount that rises steadily is in direct proportion, and taking every steady rise to be proportional is a common misconception.[^3] A £40 call-out plus £30 an hour rises by £30 every hour, but 2 hours cost £100 and 4 hours cost £160, not £200, because the call-out is paid once. Doubling the bill would pay it twice. Two quick tests catch this. Doubling one amount should double the other, and 0 should go with 0, but 0 hours still costs £40. The hourly part on its own is in proportion to the hours, so take the fixed part off, scale the rest and add it back. 5 hours cost £40 + 5 × £30 = £190.

**Two amounts are in direct proportion when doubling one doubles the other and 0 goes with 0, like a transformer's secondary voltage and its primary. A fixed charge plus a rate rises steadily but is not in proportion, so take the fixed part off before you scale.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** Test before you scale. Double one amount and see whether the other doubles, and check that 0 goes with 0. If there is a fixed part, take it off, scale the rest, then add it back.

**Worked example:** A 10 : 1 transformer has 230 V on its primary. 230 is 10 × 23, so both parts of 10 : 1 are × 23, and the secondary has 1 × 23 = 23 V. As a check, 23 × 10 = 230.

**Common mistakes**
- Scaling a fixed charge with the rest. A £40 call-out plus £30 an hour costs £130 for 3 hours, but 6 hours cost £40 + 6 × £30 = £220, not 2 × £130 = £260.
- Adding the same rise to both. On a 10 : 1 transformer, a rise of 100 V on the primary is a rise of 10 V on the secondary, not 100 V.
- Reading the ratio the wrong way round. On a 10 : 1 transformer the primary is ten times the secondary, so 11.5 V out needs 115 V in, not 1.15 V.
- Forgetting to add the fixed part back. A 3 kg drum holding 50 m of cable weighs 8 kg, so 100 m of that cable weigh 10 kg, and the drum and cable together 13 kg.

interactive.title: Direct proportion
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is two amounts kept in step, the same × on both rows of a ratio table and 0 over 0 on two locked scales, when you test whether two amounts are in direct proportion and scale from one to the other, while a fixed charge plus a rate rises steadily but pays its fixed part twice when the bill is doubled.

checks.label: When two variables are directly proportional they increase at the same rate: if the first is doubled, the other is also doubled. 100 V, 200 V and 400 V on a 10 : 1 transformer give 10 V, 20 V and 40 V, and wherever the mark is dragged, twice the primary gives twice the secondary

The turns ratio of any given transformer will be the same as its voltage ratio, so on a 10 : 1 transformer 230 V on the primary gives 230 ÷ 10 = 23 V, a rise of 100 V on the primary is a rise of 10 V on the secondary, and 11.5 V on the secondary needs 11.5 × 10 = 115 V

A fixed charge plus a rate rises steadily but is not in direct proportion: £40 plus £30 an hour costs £40 at 0 hours and £30 more each hour, and for every whole number of hours from 1 to 10, twice the hours costs £40 less than twice the bill, the call-out paid once; so 2 hours at £100 to 4 hours at £160 is × 2 on the hours but × 1.6 on the cost

Only Firm B is in direct proportion: it charges £0 at 0 hours and twice as much for twice the hours (£35, £70, £105); Firms A (£45, £80, £115) and C (£60, £90, £120) rise by the same amount each hour but work back to £10 and £30 at 0 hours, so twice the hours does not cost twice as much

Taking the fixed part off leaves an amount in proportion: 5 hours cost £40 + 5 × £30 = £190; 50 m of cable on a 3 kg drum weighing 8 kg is 5 kg of cable, so 100 m on it weigh 3 + 2 × 5 = 13 kg; the van hire's 2 extra days cost £145 − £85 = £60, so a day is £30, the fee £85 − £60 = £25, and 6 days £25 + 6 × £30 = £205

Each puzzle accepts only its own answer, worked out by its rule, and every wrong answer offered is the one a named slip gives: the ratio read backwards, the gap between its parts kept as if adding, the same rise on both scales, the rise × 10, a whole bill scaled with its fixed part, the fixed part left out, two bills added so the fixed part is paid twice, or a firm whose price rises steadily but has a fixed part

The two scales stay locked: wherever the mark can be dragged, from 0 to 400 V in steps of 10 V, its dots on both lines sit at the same point and its labels read the primary's voltage and a tenth of it, 0 V over 0 V at the left

Every picture is drawn to scale, finished: each row of blocks is its fixed part and one block for each hour, day or 50 m, as long as its total and tagged with it, the doubled bill with two call-outs; each table and scale shows the amounts the working gives

Before an answer, nothing in a puzzle's picture shows its answer: no cell, label or tag gives the missing voltage, its step, the secondary's rise or its reading at 300 V, a total asked for, a firm's price at 0 hours, or the worth of a block still to be found, and no working is written

Every demonstration has finished arriving within 3 to 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion within 2.5 s; parts start at least 0.45 s apart, each once the travel before it has ended; a counted travel holds each voltage at least 0.2 s

applied.problem: "Increase at the same rate" reads as rising by the same amount, the additive slip the course fights, and clashes with 100 V in being 10 V out; and it is the hourly part of the cost, not "the hours on their own", that is in proportion to the hours.

Voltage ratio equals turns ratio exactly only for an ideal transformer: a real secondary drops a little under load, and the scales run to 400 V on a transformer that also takes 230 V; say what the picture leaves out so explain and practice stay true of real ones.

notes.problem: Every number is kind "constant" with no source, but the call-out, hourly rate, firms' prices, drum, van hire and the 230 V, 11.5 V and 0 to 400 V voltages are values chosen for the example (assumed), with each answer computed from them; none is a real-world constant.

The fourth common mistake, forgetting to add the fixed part back, is a likely slip but no source names it (the NCETM misconception is treating a linear link as proportional); it may stay as a check but is not a documented mistake.
